anchor: Palle Torsson's Queer 3D World course (Konstfack, three weeks, 2024 intro): the three layers of Ada Research, FOUNDATION (the lab), THE UNCANNY AND ALGORITHMIC DEBT, and ONTOLOGY (hybrid and impossible space), used as the macro-structure; scanned and sculpted bodies from week 1; AI-assisted code as practice; a mini project shown to the class.
title: Three Layers: bodies in the lab, bodies in debt, bodies out of bounds
thesis: This course is built like the Queer 3D World course: three layers, like an onion. Part I is the lab. You build bodies that hold still (a point, a line, a grid, a surface, a family of colours, a body type) and learn how each one is made. Part II is the uncanny. The same bodies start to move, fall, hang, sound, scatter and grow, and every one of those motions is an approximation that owes something: time chopped into frames, forces added up step by step, solvers that stop at 'good enough', chance that is only pseudo, noise that makes everything look like a blob, recursion that must be stopped, surfaces looked up in a table, models that learn their data's bias. Part III leaves the lab: your bodies are lost in generated worlds, go soft, grow skins, get cut and joined, swarm, become impossible from all but one eye, drift from order to entropy, and finally leave the computer as a build other people can walk into. Every chapter still passes through all three layers on a small scale: make the body, read its debt, give it a place. Your own scanned or sculpted body arrives on day one and comes back in every part, so the course is one body picking up a year of procedures. The order follows the Ada spine where the spine's order is the order your hands need, and says so where it does not: chance appears early as a value and returns later as debt, isosurfaces and machine learning close the debt part, and graphs follow the maze that needs them.

parts.title: I. Foundation: the lab
parts.promise: You can build a still body in code (points, lines, grids, surfaces, colours, patterns, classes), give it a boundary and a place, turn it into a family with @export, and argue one axis with a predicted comparison sheet. Your scanned body stands among them.

parts.title: II. The uncanny and algorithmic debt
parts.promise: You can make bodies move, hang, sound, scatter and grow, and for each procedure you can say what its approximation owes or hides (frames, integration, relaxation, sampling, pseudo-randomness, the blob, the pixel, the rule, the stopped recursion, the lookup table, the bias) and show it in one still.

parts.title: III. Ontology: out of bounds
parts.promise: Your bodies leave the lab: generated worlds you can get lost in, soft and patterned skins, collages, swarms, impossible viewpoints and order-to-entropy, ending in a build other people can walk, carry or become.

tracks.title: Queer 3D World in three weeks
tracks.length: 3 weeks (15 days: taught sessions plus own work, as in the 2024 course)
tracks.mini_project: 'The body the scanner could not see': a hybrid body, your scan or sculpt collaged with ONE procedural family, standing in a small room where a visitor can meet it (stand on it, walk through it, carry it or become it). Shown to the class as a desktop build (and on the headset if it holds frame rate), with a 3-5 variant comparison sheet, a prediction written before the render, a one-sentence claim, and one debt comment in the code saying what the approximation owes. Designed first: every short-track chapter ends in a step of it. Week 1 FOUNDATION: Mon c01 scan day; Tue c02 + c03; Wed c04 headset day; Thu c07 grid + AI protocol; Fri own work (plinth). Week 2 DEBT: Mon c11 family; Tue c21 noise on your scan; Wed c22 shader skin; Thu c15 specimen sheet and the brief (pivot); Fri own work. Week 3 ONTOLOGY: Mon c33 collage; Tue-Wed own work and a guest; Thu c37 build; Fri the show. Supplied and named (the prerequisites the short track skips): the Day Zero base scene; the first-person walker and XR rig (vr_staging.tscn, XR Tools pickup), used before they are opened in c17; segment.gd show_between(); errors are met as the daily planted bug instead of c05; arrays, conditions and input stay inside the supplied walker and grid kit (c06); random values and seeds come as the FastNoiseLite seed property (c08, c20); areas and signals come in the supplied comment box and teleporter (c09); a MeshDataTool helper that displaces a scan along its normals replaces the mesh chapters (c13); a shader template with a named amplitude uniform; the sheet camera script; a CSG kit; export presets. Classes (c12) are skipped: @export works on a plain script.

tracks.title: Three Layers: the year
tracks.length: about one academic year (about 36 teaching weeks: Part I autumn, Part II winter, Part III spring, with a pause week after each synthesis)
tracks.mini_project: The short track's mini project, extended into the capstone: the same body carried through the year (after Learning Processing's Zoog and The Nature of Code's Ecosystem Project), now a room of hybrid bodies in your hall of the endless museum that is also a small complete game: player, input, camera, UI, save/load, audio and a build. Milestones: c15 first sheet and brief; c28 debt audit, recipe saved as .tres, mid-year review; c33 published JSON remix; c35 capstone proposal (two units before the end, after Aesthetic Programming ch9); c37 show and hand-over. Pause weeks with no new code idea come after c15 and c28 (after Aesthetic Programming) and give the declared returns their place.

chapters.title: Bring a body: a scan meets a point
chapters.body: Your own body, or an object you own, scanned with a phone photogrammetry app or drawn in Tilt Brush / Open Brush, exported as .glb and dropped at 1:1 into the Day Zero base scene next to one point; a one-line script prints a greeting and the body's name to the Output panel.

argument.axis: triangles in the scan (set with Blender's Decimate modifier before export)
argument.predict: 100k and 10k will look most alike from 2 m: the body covers fewer screen pixels than 10k triangles have faces. The break comes between 1k and 200, where the silhouette turns into facets.
argument.claim: Below about a thousand triangles a scanned body stops reading as a person and starts reading as a polyhedron; above about ten thousand the extra triangles are invisible from where a visitor stands.

chapters.debt: A scan is a reconstruction, not a recording: holes where the camera did not look, light baked into the texture, the back you never captured, surfaces averaged from many photos. Photogrammetry fails on dark, shiny, hairy and moving surfaces [mem], so who and what scans well is not neutral. This is the course description's own triad: stretchability, topology, bias ('töjbarhet, topologier, bias' [V]).
chapters.place: Stand beside your double at 1:1 in a room it never stood in; walk around it and find the side the scanner missed. XR route (supplied rig): see it at your own eye height.

lineage.processing: LP ch1-2 (pixels; running a sketch); Handbook Structure 1 (code elements)
lineage.application_wp: polycount against smooth deformation (application l.89) met on day one
lineage.klee: before I.1: the body as given, before the point sets off
lineage.reference: Queer 3D World week 1 (3D scanning, Tilt Brush, export to Blender) [V]; UCSC AGPM 129 'make before the tool'; Anthropy's Twine book shares a work in chapter 1

chapters.departure: Adds a strand the spine does not have: bringing in a scanned or sculpted body, the Queer 3D course's first day. Primitives_Ignorance (the tenth primitives hall) is visited on day one as a field trip because it asks the same polycount question of a sphere.
chapters.project_step: Mini project, day 1: choose the body you will carry all course (scan, sculpt or found model) and keep its four decimation levels.

chapters.title: The engine calls you: a point that lives
chapters.body: A point: a supplied MeshInstance3D with a SphereMesh whose radius and position your script sets in _ready(); a counter raised in _process() shows on a Label3D (the point-zero kit).

argument.predict: 0.005 and 0.02 will look most alike from 2 m, both a dot; 0.1 already reads as a ball and 0.5 as a body you could bump into.
argument.claim: A mathematical point has no size but a drawn one must: at arm's length the dot turns into a ball somewhere between 2 and 10 cm.

chapters.debt: The engine cannot draw nothing: the 'point' is a sphere of 32 x 16 segments, about a thousand triangles standing in for zero size. And the counter counts frames, not seconds; on a faster screen it runs faster. That debt is repaid with delta in chapter 16.
chapters.place: Walk to the point and through it: it has no boundary yet, so your walker passes through it like a ghost.

lineage.processing: LP ch3-4 (setup/draw = _ready/_process; variables); Handbook Data 1
lineage.application_wp: not listed (a basic element no work package names)
lineage.klee: I.1 the dot before its walk
lineage.reference: Queer 3D Foundation layer, 'a typical science lab' [V]; Learn GDScript From Zero lessons 1-10 (statements before the game loop)

chapters.project_step: Put a point at a landmark on your scanned body (the nose, a knuckle) from code; its radius is your first variable.

chapters.title: Solid or ghost: what you see and what stops you
chapters.body: Three points built entirely in code (SphereMesh.new(), MeshInstance3D.new(), StaticBody3D + CollisionShape3D + SphereShape3D, add_child), one visible radius and a different boundary each.

argument.axis: collider radius as a fraction of the visible radius (Debug > Visible Collision Shapes on)
argument.predict: 'none', '0.5x' and '1x' will look identical in a still without the debug overlay; with it, 1x and 0.5x are the closest pair. The boundary is invisible to the camera.
argument.claim: What you see and what stops you are two different bodies; a still shows the second only when a debug overlay draws it.

chapters.debt: The collider is a second, simpler body the eye never sees. Every game body is a pair, a picture and a boundary, and they are allowed to disagree. First critique of a starter (after Montfort's 'Critique My Starter Programs'): which bodies does Godot give you by default (the capsule, the cube) and who are they for?
chapters.place: Walk into each point: pass through the ghost, stop at the solid, and be stopped early by the 2x boundary, an invisible wall around a body larger than it looks.

lineage.processing: LP ch8 as a user (objects you call but did not write); Handbook Shape 1
lineage.klee: I.2-I.4 active, medial and passive: the point that acts and the point acted upon
lineage.reference: Point One's solid/ghost distinction; Gaboury, Image Objects ch3 (the Utah teapot: which bodies are default); Queer 3D: the lab 'also has something uncanny' [V]

chapters.project_step: Give your scanned body a boundary two ways (the automatic convex shape, a hand-sized box); walk into both and note where picture and boundary disagree.

chapters.title: Where is a body? Coordinates, frames and the hand
chapters.body: A constellation of points as children of one parent Node3D; you move, rotate and scale the parent and watch position (local) and global_position (world) disagree.

argument.predict: 1 and 2 will look most alike in a framed still (same shape, the camera reframes); at 0.25 the constellation is a jewel, at 4 it is a room you stand inside.
argument.claim: A body's numbers are relative to its parent: the same local coordinates make a jewel or a room depending on one frame above them.

chapters.debt: 'Where' always means 'where relative to what'. The world origin is a convention, and far from it float precision starts to jitter [mem]. A carried object is re-parented to the hand: a second frame the code must know about.
chapters.place: Carry it. On the XR route pick up a point with the supplied XR Tools pickup (ruling: pickup belongs to Point Coordinates); on desktop, the supplied crosshair carry. Scale the parent to 4 and stand inside your own constellation.

lineage.processing: LP ch14 transformations, met ten chapters early because a Godot node IS a transform
lineage.application_wp: 'noise and vectors' as basic concepts (application l.9)
lineage.klee: II.14-II.17 dimension; the viewer's shifting axis
lineage.reference: Queer 3D week 2 'VR in Unity' [V] moved to week 1; research_creative: transform early is where agreeing with the spine is right

chapters.project_step: Parent your scan and your points to one Node3D; keep stills at scale 0.25 and 4.

chapters.title: Two points make a relation: the line
chapters.body: A line body: a thin box stretched between two carried points by the supplied show_between() (segment.gd), with b - a and its length printed while either end moves.

argument.axis: line thickness as a fraction of its length
argument.predict: 0.002 and 0.01 will look most alike (both a drawn mark); at 0.25 the 'line' is a beam you could stand on.
argument.claim: A line in 3D is a stretched body: its thickness decides whether it reads as a mark, a rod or a beam.

chapters.debt: Break it on purpose (the W01 workshop): predict each error before running (a typo, a null node, a method that does not exist), then read Godot's exact message and the class reference. 'Valid and intentional are different' (Montfort). The line is a box pretending to have one dimension.
chapters.place: Carry the two ends apart until the line crosses the room; walk under the beam version.

lineage.processing: LP ch2 errors, ch5 expressions; Handbook Math 1
lineage.klee: I.2 a line limited by two fixed points
lineage.reference: Montfort, Exploratory Programming ch4; GDQuest's lesson 2 'your first error'; ruling: distance belongs to Point Lines

chapters.project_step: Draw three lines from code between landmarks on your scanned body, a skeleton of distances, and print their lengths.

chapters.title: Klee's walk: the trace
chapters.body: A recorder: while a named input action is held, the carried point appends its position to an Array[Vector3] only if it has moved more than a gate distance; each kept position becomes a small sphere (the point-trace kit).

argument.axis: gate distance (m) before a new position is kept
argument.predict: 0.005 and 0.02 will look most alike, both a continuous line; at 0.4 the trace becomes separate stepping stones.
argument.claim: A trace is a sampling: the gate decides whether a walk is kept as a line or as a row of stones.

chapters.debt: The walk is continuous and the list is not: everything between two kept samples is lost, and a capped list forgets its own beginning (pop_front). The condition is taught before the distance threshold (standing ruling).
chapters.place: Walk while holding the action: your own route becomes a line you can later walk back along.

lineage.processing: LP ch5 conditionals, ch9 arrays (mouse history); Handbook Control 1, Data 4
lineage.klee: I.1 'an active line on a walk'
lineage.reference: Queer 3D Foundation question 'how do points, lines and the grid work' [V]; rulings: list before append, condition before a distance threshold

chapters.project_step: Walk around your scanned body holding the action: the first thing in your hall made by your own movement.

chapters.title: Many bodies: the grid as an instruction
chapters.body: A floor of cubes built by two nested for-loops, each cube with a collider: first written as a LeWitt-style instruction in plain words, then generated by an AI assistant, then read, run and corrected by you.

argument.axis: gap between cells as a fraction of the cell size
argument.predict: 0 and 0.05 will look most alike from standing height (a floor with seams); the break is between 0.3 and 1.0, where the floor turns into stepping stones.
argument.claim: Repetition becomes structure when the gap is smaller than the foot: one loop makes a floor or a set of stones.

chapters.debt: The AI protocol, after LeWitt's instruction-as-work: write the instruction, predict the grid, ask the AI, run it, and mark every place the AI had to guess (cell size? corner or centre origin? which axis is up?). The guesses are the debt. Write down what must not change and which observation would prove the code wrong.
chapters.place: Stand on it, then cross it at each gap: at which gap does your walker fall through?
godot: any AI assistant, with the instruction kept as a comment above the code

lineage.processing: LP ch6 loops (nested grid); DBN 'Line' then 'Lines'; Handbook Control 2
lineage.klee: I.5-I.6 'purely repetitive and therefore structural'; the chessboard
lineage.reference: Queer 3D course description: 'use ChatGPT to write simpler programs that can activate and generate 3D' [V]; LeWitt; research_bauhaus's ai_assist protocol; ruling: grids are not prerequisites for the first line

chapters.project_step: Build a plinth or floor for your body out of a loop and decide its gap.

chapters.title: Chance as a value: Schotter
chapters.body: Nees's Schotter as a walkable floor: a grid of slabs whose random rotation and offset grow row by row (lerp from 0 to a maximum), plus a 10 PRINT row where randf() < 0.5 chooses one of two diagonals (Array's molnar_cube_study carries the same disorder on a lattice).

argument.axis: maximum disorder at the last row (radians)
argument.predict: 0 and 0.2 will look most alike: a little disorder still reads as a grid. The grid 'breaks' somewhere past 0.6.
argument.claim: Randomness needs a regular grid to be seen: the row where the grid stops reading as a grid is where chance becomes the subject.

chapters.debt: Unseeded randf() gives a new floor every run, so no still can be repeated; that debt is repaid in chapter 20. Nake's Hommage à Paul Klee (1965) asks whether a random number can stand in for intuition.
chapters.place: Walk down the Schotter floor: at which row does the disorder make it unwalkable?

lineage.processing: LP ch4 random() as a value; Handbook Math 4 Random
lineage.noc: NoC 0 met as a value only
lineage.application_wp: WP1 Basic Elements begins with randomness
lineage.klee: Klee has no chance; Nake adds it to Klee's 'Hauptweg und Nebenwege'
lineage.reference: Queer 3D Foundation's first question: 'what is randomness and how can it be visualised?' [V]; 10 PRINT's 'Regularity' before 'Randomness'; Recreating the Past week 1 (Molnar)

chapters.departure: Randomness (spine 10) is met early, at array_tutorial's place (3), as a VALUE disturbing a grid already built: the Queer 3D course asks it first, the application puts it in WP1, and every creative-coding tradition meets random() early. Randomness as a TOPIC keeps its spine place in chapter 20, as a declared return.
chapters.project_step: Scatter ten copies of a small primitive around your scan with a disorder ramp; note which amount still reads as arranged.

chapters.title: A body that notices: the floor that answers
chapters.body: The Schotter floor again, now with an Area3D over each slab: when your walker enters, the slab emits a signal, lights up, and a moment later is freed.

argument.axis: fraction of stepped-on slabs that vanish
argument.predict: 0 and 0.1 will look most alike in a still taken after a walk (a floor with a few holes); at 0.7 your path is printed as an absence.
argument.claim: A floor that answers keeps a negative trace: after the walk, the holes are a picture of where a body went.

chapters.debt: A signal is only as wide as its area: a body moving far enough between two physics frames can skip it. A freed node is gone; nothing remembers it unless you record it.
chapters.place: Walk it: the floor disappears behind you, Klee's walk inverted into a missing floor.

lineage.processing: LP ch3 interaction (events); Handbook Input 1-2
lineage.klee: I.1 the walk, as removal
lineage.reference: Squash the Creeps parts 6-7 (areas, signals) as the game kit's first event; Queer 3D: the uncanny inside the lab

chapters.departure: Random_Remove (spine 10) carries a Part I chapter because the first event a body meets should be a floor responding to it; its seeded draw waits for chapter 20.
chapters.project_step: Give your hall one thing that notices the visitor near your body (light now, sound in chapter 19).

chapters.title: A body of parts: pivots and frames
chapters.body: A limb of three segments, each a child of the one before (bone, tendon, muscle after Klee I.9), posed by setting each joint's Basis from an angle.

argument.axis: pivot position along each segment (0 = base, 1 = tip)
argument.predict: 0 and 0.5 will look most alike at small angles; at 1.5 the pivot sits outside the segment and the limb swings like a door instead of bending.
argument.claim: A body of parts is a tree of frames: where the pivot sits decides whether it bends like a limb or swings like a door.

chapters.debt: A Basis mixes rotation and scale: scale a parent unevenly and every child shears. Euler angles hide gimbal lock (Random_Rotate_Random_XYZ). A hierarchy always has a parent. Klee's own passage maps active/passive organs onto male/female: name that as the dark spot of the source this course 'puts in drag'.
chapters.place: Ride it: stand on the carousel (Trans_Rotation) or pass the slatted wall that opens as you approach (Trans_Body). Pose a limb from your scan's shoulder.
godot: a pivot as an offset child

lineage.processing: LP ch14 push/pop, rotate about a pivot; Handbook Transform 1-2
lineage.klee: I.9-I.10 bone, ligament, tendon, muscle as active, medial and passive organs
lineage.reference: Queer 3D lineage: Bellmer's jointed doll, collage and hybrid form [V]; Form+Code puts Repeat before Transform

chapters.departure: Transformation (spine 2) comes after array_tutorial (3): a body of parts needs many parts first (Form+Code's Repeat before Transform), and position and frame were met in chapter 4.
chapters.project_step: Attach a jointed appendage built from primitives to your scan (Code as Creative Medium's 'Personal Prosthetic').

chapters.title: Colour as a family: the first @export
chapters.body: An arch of N bands, each a primitive with its own StandardMaterial3D coloured by Color.from_hsv(i / N, s, v); N is an @export, so the Inspector turns one script into a family, and make_band(i) is your first own function.

argument.predict: 12 and 48 will look most alike: above about twelve the eye stops counting bands and sees a gradient.
argument.claim: Quantity turns into continuity: above about twelve bands the arch stops being a sequence of colours and becomes one gradient.

chapters.debt: HSV is a model, not the eye: equal hue steps are not equal perceived steps (the yellow band looks brighter), and the material colour is not the screen colour (light, tonemapping, sRGB). Albers: a colour has many faces.
chapters.place: Walk through the arch; change its light (Color_Flashlight) and watch the family change with no change to the code.

lineage.processing: LP ch1 RGB, ch7 functions; Handbook Color 1
lineage.klee: IV.43 the colour circle, met here as appearance; its energy returns in chapter 22
lineage.reference: Albers, Interaction of Color ('make two colours look alike'); Aesthetic Programming ch2; ICM's double titles ('A family: @export')

chapters.project_step: Expose one @export on your body's material (hue, saturation or banding) and render three values side by side.

chapters.title: A body type: the class that crosses a category
chapters.body: 'Describe a body in a single class': class_name Pyramid with typed @exports base_sides: int and height: float; the base ring is placed with cos/sin in a loop and joined to the apex with the line helper from chapter 5 (a wireframe body; faces come in chapter 13).

argument.predict: 12 and 48 will look most alike, both a cone. 3 and 4 differ most in name (tetrahedron, pyramid) and least in number.
argument.claim: With enough sides a pyramid is a cone: one integer parameter crosses a named category, and nothing in the class marks where.

chapters.debt: The circle is never drawn, only approximated by n sides (Primitives_Portals: circular approximation and limits). The class decides which properties a body has, so it decides what can vary: the modelling choice is the critique.
chapters.place: Carry the pieces of Melencolia's snap pyramid and assemble a body you then stand inside at 1:1.

lineage.processing: LP ch8 objects (Zoog as a class), ch13 trig; Handbook Shape 3 Parameters
lineage.klee: I.7 proportion (2:3:5, the golden section)
lineage.reference: CCSWG 2024 'describe war in a single class', turned to bodies; Queer 3D debt: algorithms taken for granted are simplifications [V]

chapters.departure: Returns to primitives halls (Melencolia, Portals) after colour: the class and the circle's approximation need @export and functions first.
chapters.project_step: Wrap your body's procedural part in a class with two typed @exports.

chapters.title: Surfaces from vertices: can you stand on it?
chapters.body: A triangle from three Vector3s, then a heightfield y = sin(x) cos(z) built with SurfaceTool on an n x n grid, generate_normals(), and a trimesh collider made from the same vertices.

argument.predict: 8 and 32 will look most alike from standing height with smooth normals; 2 is a folded plane, not a wave.
argument.claim: The surface you walk on and the surface you see are one list of vertices: at low resolution you walk on a polyhedron, not on the wave.

chapters.debt: Smooth normals lie about the shape: they make 8 look like 32 while the collider keeps 8's facets (roll a ball and it bumps). Winding order decides which side exists: Godot winds front faces clockwise.
chapters.place: Stand on it; drop spheres and watch them roll over facets you cannot see.

lineage.processing: LP ch14 vertex shapes; Handbook Shape 2 Vertices; PShape
lineage.klee: I.3-I.4 medial lines whose figures read as planes
lineage.reference: Catlike Coding Basics 2-3 (a graph becomes a surface); Moholy-Nagy material, then volume; Queer 3D debt 'deformation and polygon count' [V]

chapters.departure: WaveFunctions_Sine_Space (spine 9) is visited early as 'the graph', following the engine tradition's graph-to-surface ladder; the wave sequence keeps its place in chapter 19.
chapters.project_step: Build your hall's floor from a function and check that your scan's feet meet it.

chapters.title: The tile and its repeats
chapters.body: A 4 x 4 motif and a function get_color(x, y) -> Color that returns it under a repeat rule, baked into an Image and wrapped as a texture on a floor and on your chapter-13 surface.

argument.predict: pm and pg will look most alike if the motif is itself mirror-symmetric: on a symmetric tile the glide is invisible.
argument.claim: Two symmetry rules can make the same floor: the group you see depends on the motif as much as on the rule.

chapters.debt: Texture filtering: nearest against linear blurs the seams, mipmaps turn a fine pattern grey from standing height, and UVs stretch on a curved surface (the Ribbon halls).
chapters.place: Walk on the patterned floor; lay the pattern on your wave surface and find where it stretches.
godot: func get_color(x: int, y: int) -> Color

lineage.processing: LP ch15 images and pixels; Handbook Image 1
lineage.application_wp: WP3 pattern and world building, named early
lineage.klee: I.6 the chessboard: structure as repetition
lineage.reference: Book of Shaders ch9 Patterns; Queer 3D lineage: Escher's Metamorphosis [V]; Albers's 'two different colours look alike' turned into a symmetry problem

chapters.project_step: Give your body a patterned skin or plinth with one repeat rule.

chapters.title: Synthesis I: the specimen sheet
chapters.body: Your hybrid so far (the scan plus one procedural family) saved as a PackedScene, instanced four times at four values of one @export, lined up, put in a group, and photographed by a supplied sheet camera into one PNG in user://.

argument.axis: share of the body that is procedural
argument.predict: 'scan only' and 'scan + one part' will look most alike: a small procedural part reads as an accessory until it changes the silhouette.
argument.claim: A hybrid reads as a new body only once the procedural part changes the silhouette; before that it reads as a costume.

chapters.debt: The sheet shows one standpoint, and a family that changes on a face the camera does not see will look inert (Ada's own measurement: five of seven 'dead' DNA verdicts were false). Write the ReadMe beside the code and one debt comment inside it.
chapters.place: Your hall: the four instances stand in a row in your room of the endless museum; walk the row at visitor height.

lineage.processing: Handbook Synthesis 1 (form and code); LP lesson-end projects
lineage.noc: NoC's Ecosystem Project step (a creature for a museum)
lineage.klee: the part-end key sentence
lineage.reference: Queer 3D mini project shown to the class [V]; Generative Design's numbered variants; Ada's DNA sheets and dna.predicted_degeneracy; Aesthetic Programming RunMe/ReadMe

chapters.departure: A synthesis chapter: it returns to colour (spine 4) and primitives (1) halls after tiling (5) because it gathers Part I, not because a hall needs it here.
chapters.project_step: SHORT TRACK PIVOT (end of week 2): write the mini-project brief (body, axis, prediction, place) and render the first sheet.

chapters.title: Time in slices: the staircase under the curve
chapters.body: A Riemann staircase: n pillars under a curve, rebuilt live in the editor by an @tool script whenever n's setter runs; then the curve set moving with delta so it keeps one speed on any screen.

argument.predict: 8 and 64 will look most alike from across the hall; up close 64 is a ramp and 8 is still a stair.
argument.claim: The staircase approaches the curve and never becomes it: the approximation's debt shrinks with n and never reaches zero.

chapters.debt: The frame is the computer's slice of time. _process runs once per frame, so chapter 2's counter counted frames; delta pays that back. The integral is a sum and the curve on screen is a polyline. Part I's bodies held still; from here everything moves, and every motion is sampled.
chapters.place: Walk up the staircase at each n. With the capsule walker, at which step height does the stair stop being climbable? [mem: CharacterBody3D has no automatic step-up; the capsule's round foot climbs only small steps. Test it.]
godot: var n: int: set(v): n = v; rebuild()

lineage.processing: Handbook Structure 2 Continuous (the draw loop opens part 2)
lineage.klee: II.14 dimension: a stair between two planes
lineage.reference: Queer 3D debt: algorithms as 'negotiations with what mathematics cannot answer' [V]; the Processing Handbook's static before continuous

chapters.project_step: Make one property of your body live: a setter plus @tool, so dragging it in the Inspector rebuilds the body in the editor.

chapters.title: The integrator owes: forces, and the walker opened
chapters.body: A thrown body integrated three ways (your Euler step, your semi-implicit step, Godot's RigidBody3D), drawn as three trails beside the exact parabola; then the supplied first-person walker is opened, and its gravity turns out to be an integrator too.

argument.predict: 0.0167 and 0.004 will look most alike: over a short throw Euler's drift at 60 Hz is under a centimetre; at 0.1 the arc visibly overshoots.
argument.claim: Physics in a game is a chosen error: Euler's arc drifts from the true parabola by an amount that grows with the step.

chapters.debt: Integration error, energy from nowhere, results that depend on the physics rate (Ada measured one settling die at 15/16 at 90 Hz and 2/16 at 60 Hz [V memory file]). Critique the starter body: the walker is a 1.8 m capsule. Which body does the engine assume a player is?
chapters.place: Enter the force-as-place zone (Vectors_Act5): gravity is replaced for your walker inside it; throw parts of your body across its edge.
godot: velocity += a * delta; position += velocity * delta

chapters.project_step: Make part of your body fall, be thrown or resist: one part as a RigidBody3D, one moved by an integrator you wrote.

chapters.title: Good enough: form found by relaxation
chapters.body: A hanging net of Verlet points in a PackedVector3Array with distance constraints, relaxed a set number of iterations per frame between two anchors you can grab.

argument.predict: 10 and 50 will look most alike (the net has reached its catenary); at 1 it sags like rubber.
argument.claim: The solver stops when the error is invisible, not when it is zero, and the frame budget decides where that is.

chapters.debt: 'Good enough' is a decision: iterations cost milliseconds (read them in the Profiler), and stiffness here is a side effect of the iteration count, not a material. Von Neumann, quoted in the Queer 3D intro: truth is too complicated for anything but approximations [V].
chapters.place: Grab an anchor and walk; the net follows. Walk under the catenary arch (FormFinding_Catenary).

chapters.title: Pendulum, circle, spiral: sampled waves and sound
chapters.body: Klee's derivation in code: a pendulum's swing, the same motion as a point going round a circle, and a spiral whose radius grows every turn, swept into a walkable staircase; each crossing plays a tone rendered sample by sample.

argument.predict: 0 (a circle) and 0.2 will look most alike near the start, seen from above; -0.2 closes toward a point and 0.6 flings outward.
argument.claim: One parameter turns the circle into Klee's two spirals: negative growth contracts toward a point, positive growth expands without end.

chapters.debt: Sound is a list of samples: 44,100 numbers a second stand in for a continuous wave, and with too few, high frequencies fold back as false tones (aliasing). The spiral is a polyline, the pendulum an integrator (chapter 17), and a Timer fires on the first frame after it is due, not at the moment.
chapters.place: Climb the spiral staircase (Sky_Stairs); stand at the pendulum's crossing and hear it.

chapters.title: Pseudo: the seed returns
chapters.body: Chapter 8's Schotter floor rebuilt with a RandomNumberGenerator whose seed you choose, save to user:// and load after a restart, so the same 'random' floor comes back.

argument.predict: '1959' and '1959 after a restart' will be identical pixel for pixel; 1959 and 1960 are as different as any two random floors.
argument.claim: Chance under a seed is a pattern that returns: two runs with one seed are one picture.

chapters.debt: Code-critique station (after Critical Code Studies' Kittler chapter): read and annotate about 20 lines of seed_replay_demo and write what 'random' means there. Pseudo-randomness is a deterministic function; a die thrown with a seeded velocity can still land differently at another physics rate. Chun's 'sourcery': reading the script does not show the generator inside the engine.
chapters.place: Throw the seeded die (Random_Cubes) and predict its face; walk the floor that returns.

chapters.title: Noise: chance with memory, and the blob
chapters.body: Your scan's vertices pushed along their normals by FastNoiseLite (a supplied MeshDataTool helper in the short track), and a noise field of 10,000 cubes drawn as one MultiMesh.

argument.predict: simplex and perlin will look most alike: both are gradient noises with the rounded 'blob' look; cellular breaks it with ridges and cells.
argument.claim: The 'blob aesthetic' belongs to gradient noise, not to noise as such: change the generator and the body stops looking melted.

chapters.debt: The Queer 3D intro names it: noise algorithms produced a 'blob aesthetic' [V]. Noise is smoothed pseudo-randomness under a seed (chapter 20), and octaves finer than a pixel are paid for and never seen (Noise_Space_10's own source comment explains why its ladder stops at four [V via maps/ada.json]).
chapters.place: Walk the noise terrain (Noise_Space_10); stand next to your blobbed double.

chapters.title: Shaders: the pixel computes, the collider stays
chapters.body: A rubber skin for your body: a spatial shader that displaces vertices by a wave or fBm in vertex() and draws a fresnel rim in fragment(), its amplitude a uniform set from GDScript.

argument.predict: 0 and 0.02 will look most alike in a still; at 0.4 the picture has left the collider 40 cm behind.
argument.claim: A shader can move a body's picture as far as it likes while the collider stays where the CPU put it: what you see and what stops you split again.

chapters.debt: The GPU computes every pixel and the CPU never sees the result: chapter 3's solid and ghost at a new scale (Shader_09's hook: visible deformation, unchanged collision). Colour returns as energy (Klee IV). Steyerl's poor image: resolution and compression are political.

chapters.title: Rules and their edge: cellular automata
chapters.body: A bridge grown from an elementary cellular automaton: each generation one row, each live cell a collidable block, computed with a current and a next buffer.

argument.predict: 30 and 110 will look most alike from a distance (irregular, full of triangles); 90 is a clean Sierpinski lattice and 184 settles into diagonal traffic.
argument.claim: Four rules on one neighbourhood: some grow a bridge you can cross, some a sieve you fall through. The rule number decides walkability.

chapters.debt: Step one generation in the debugger (a breakpoint, the remote scene tree): the second buffer is what stops a rule from reading its own half-written answer. At the edge of chaos one flipped cell (CA_EdgeOfChaos) spreads or dies, and you cannot know which without running it.
chapters.place: Walk the CA bridge; where the rule leaves gaps, you fall.

MultiMesh display + BoxShape3D per live cell

chapters.title: Recursion must be stopped: fractal bodies
chapters.body: Munari's tree: one rule (each branch splits in two, each thinner than the one before) as a recursive function with an explicit depth limit and one seeded 'mad branch'.

argument.predict: 6 and 9 will look most alike from standing height (the new twigs are smaller than a pixel), while 9 has eight times the branches.
argument.claim: Recursion's debt is paid in invisible work: past depth 6 the tree costs more and looks the same.

chapters.debt: 'Recursion must always be controlled' (the Queer 3D intro [V]): plant the missing base case and read the stack-overflow message. Munari's mad branch as a queer reading of recursion: the family still reads through the exception.

chapters.title: Grammar: the turtle, its stack, and the building
chapters.body: An L-system: an axiom string rewritten by a Dictionary of rules, read by a turtle (Klee's walking point as Logo) that pushes and pops its state on a stack, drawn as lines and built as walkable corridors.

argument.predict: 18 and 25.7 will look most alike (both plants); 90 turns the same grammar into a floor plan.
argument.claim: One grammar is a plant at 25 degrees and a building at 90: the interpretation, not the rule, decides the category.

chapters.debt: Strings grow exponentially, so a symbol budget has to stop the rewriting (the grammar's debt). The turtle's stack is a memory of where it was, and a pop throws it away.
chapters.place: Walk the grammar's corridors (LSystems_Architecture): a building that is also a plant.

chapters.title: Implicit bodies: the lookup table and the neck
chapters.body: A body with no vertices of its own: a density field from two to five sources joined by a smooth minimum, meshed by marching cubes with the case table supplied, then tested for holes.

argument.axis: smooth-minimum blend radius k (m), sources 0.5 m apart
argument.predict: 0 and 0.1 will look most alike (two separate bodies); a neck appears near 0.3 and at 0.8 they are one blob.
argument.claim: The blob is a parameter: once k exceeds the gap between sources, two bodies become one.

chapters.debt: Code-critique station: read the supplied case table, a finite negotiation with a continuous surface in which ambiguous cases are settled by convention. A test that every edge is shared by exactly two triangles shows where the table leaves holes. Quilez's smooth minimum is where the blob aesthetic comes from.
chapters.place: Walk into the cave (ISO_Caves); stand in the neck between two sources.

chapters.title: Bias: the model is a picture of its data
chapters.body: A k-nearest-neighbour classifier painted on the floor: labelled bodies you made stand on it, every floor pixel takes the label of its k nearest bodies (sorted by distance), and a Button steps the training.

argument.axis: share of training bodies from the majority class
argument.predict: 90/10 and 99/1 will look most alike: the minority's region has already shrunk to islands around its few examples.
argument.claim: The boundary follows the majority: a classifier is a map of its data's proportions, not of the bodies.

chapters.debt: 'Machine-learning models are always biased' (Queer 3D intro [V]). Turn it on the course itself: the AI assistant used since chapter 7 is a model trained on a corpus. Ask it for 'a human body' in code and record what it assumes (height, symmetry, two arms). Collect and label your own small data set first (Feminist Data Set).

chapters.title: A generated world you can get lost in
chapters.body: A maze carved from a seed by a depth-first walk (a stack), checked by a flood fill (a queue), then given a navigation mesh so an agent with your walker's radius can find its way through.

argument.axis: corridor width relative to the walker's diameter
argument.predict: 0.8 and 1.0 will look almost identical in plan view, yet only 1.0 is solvable for the body; 1.5 and 3.0 both read as clear mazes.
argument.claim: A maze solvable in the array can be unsolvable for a body: the route belongs to the corridor's width, not to the grid.

chapters.debt: The array's route and the body's route differ: the navigation mesh erodes every wall by the agent's radius. The application's WP3 question: how do we navigate an auto-generated world?
chapters.place: Walk it; release one navigation agent the size of your walker and one the size of your scanned body.

chapters.title: Graphs: the world as a network
chapters.body: Your maze from chapter 29 turned into a graph (cells as nodes, openings as edges); BFS, DFS and A* replayed as light moving through the corridors; closing a door re-plans the route.

argument.predict: BFS and A* will light the same final path (both shortest), but A* lights far fewer cells; DFS's path is the longest.
argument.claim: Search algorithms leave different traces in one maze: the path can be the same while what was visited differs.

chapters.debt: A graph keeps only what someone chose to connect; the rest of the world disappears from it. A* needs a heuristic, an assumption about distance that can be wrong.
chapters.place: Walk the lit path; press the button that closes a corridor and watch the route re-plan around you.

chapters.title: Soft: polycount against deformation
chapters.body: Your scan as a SoftBody3D at several decimation levels, poked by a ray from your hand or crosshair: where it is hit it dents and throws a burst of particles.

argument.axis: triangles in the scan used as a soft body
argument.predict: 3000 and 12000 will look most alike at rest, but 12000 will not hold the frame budget (or goes unstable); 200 dents in facets.
argument.claim: A soft body can bend only where it has vertices, and every vertex costs: smooth deformation and smooth surface pull against each other.

chapters.debt: The application's own question: the trade-off between polycount and deforming a body smoothly (l.89). The course description's 'stretchability' as ideology [V]: which bodies does the engine let bend, and at what price?

chapters.title: Morphogenesis: Turing's pattern on your skin
chapters.body: A Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion field on two buffers (first on a worker thread on the CPU, then as a ping-pong shader), used as the skin and displacement of your hybrid.

argument.predict: stripes and labyrinth will look most alike (both line-like); spots differ most.
argument.claim: The same two chemicals make spots or stripes from two rates alone: in Turing's model a pattern is a rate, not a blueprint.

chapters.debt: The model is a 1952 simplification that biology partly confirmed and partly refused [mem]. The CPU version stalls the frame unless it moves to a thread (and a worker task must be waited on to be released); the GPU version is fast and unreadable from GDScript.
chapters.place: Stand in a room whose walls grow the pattern (a bio-cyborg room); touch the skin to seed a new spot.

chapters.title: Cut and join: collage bodies
chapters.body: A collage body after Höch and Bellmer: your scan combined with procedural parts by union, intersection and difference; the recipe (operands, order, operation) stored as JSON so a classmate can remix it.

argument.predict: A ∪ B and A − B will look most alike from the front if B sits mostly behind A; A − B and B − A are never alike.
argument.claim: Order is part of a collage: A − B and B − A are two different bodies made from the same parts.

chapters.debt: CSG on a scanned mesh is fragile: non-manifold scans fail or take seconds. Coincident faces z-fight, and baking to a static mesh freezes the collage. JSON keeps the recipe but not the reasons.

chapters.title: Many bodies choose: swarms
chapters.body: A flock of small bodies derived from your hybrid: a base Agent class that Boid, Ant and Slime extend, steering by separation, alignment and cohesion, with the visitor as an obstacle.

argument.predict: 0 and 0.5 will look most alike (a clump); at 5 the flock dissolves into evenly spaced individuals.
argument.claim: One weight decides whether many bodies read as one body or as a crowd of individuals.

chapters.debt: All-pairs neighbour search costs n squared, so the frame budget caps the flock (a spatial hash lifts the cap). Each agent sees only what its rule lets it see. Emergence is a reading, not a property.

chapters.title: Impossible space: the camera decides

argument.claim: An impossible body is possible from exactly one eye: impossibility is a fact about a camera, not about the geometry.

chapters.title: Order to entropy: the body between states
chapters.body: Your hybrid given one λ from order (0) to entropy (1) that disorders all its families at once, and an enum state machine (jarred, released, dissolving) that tries to name what λ does.

argument.predict: 0 and 0.25 will look most alike (order is robust); the body 'flips' between 0.5 and 0.75.
argument.claim: The body keeps its category until λ crosses a threshold and then changes all at once: the edge of chaos is where a category decides.

chapters.debt: A state machine is a list of allowed identities; λ is what the enum cannot hold. The QFEP F-to-E arc is the course's own arc: the application's 'as we step towards more entropy... difference and diversity increase'.

chapters.body: Your hybrid in its room, exported as a build other people can run: a desktop build, and a Quest build if the room holds the headset's frame rate.

learned_from: Queer 3D World (Palle, 2024) [V]: the three layers become the three parts, and every chapter repeats all three on a small scale (make it, read its debt, place it); scanning on day one; 'use ChatGPT to write simpler programs' becomes a taught protocol (c07) and later an object of critique (c27); a mini project shown to the class ends both tracks.

Aesthetic Programming (Soon and Cox): a critical theme tied to each piece of syntax rather than a separate theory track; the RunMe/ReadMe pair, with Ada's falsifiable PREDICTION + CLAIM in place of open ReadMe questions; pause weeks; the final project planned two units before the end.

Critical Code Studies (Marino) and the CCSWG: code-critique stations placed at the DEBT step and never at the opening (the RNG in c20, the marching-cubes table in c26, the student's own code in c28); the confessing comment (Climategate) becomes the 'debt comment'; 'describe X in a single class' becomes c12; the critique thread maps onto Ada's forum; Taroko Gorge remixes become the JSON collage remix (c33).

Montfort, Exploratory Programming: modify before write (the runnable kits); errors taught as a positive topic ('valid and intentional are different', c05); 'Critique My Starter Programs' turned on Godot's default capsule and cube (c03, c17).

10 PRINT: 'Regularity' before 'Randomness', which is why chance first appears as disorder on a grid already built (c08, Schotter) and returns as seeds (c20); its Maze Walker becomes the walkable maze (c29).
Nake, Nees and Molnar (research_bauhaus): randomness enters the Klee lineage in 1965-68 as disturbance of an order, so it can come early without skipping the grid.

Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook, with the corrected section order [V via research_bauhaus / maps/lineage.json]: the line on a walk (c06), repetition as structure (c07), the body of bones and tendons (c10), balance and gravity (c17-c18), pendulum then circle then spiral (c19), colour as energy at the end (c22). The active/passive = male/female passage is named as a dark spot (c10).

Albers, Interaction of Color: a stated perceptual target with one constrained material is the ancestor of the ARGUMENT strand; 'make two different bodies look alike' is the prediction turned into an assignment (c11, c14).
LeWitt: the instruction as the work gives the AI-assisted protocol (write the instruction, predict, generate, check, mark where the AI had to guess) in c07.

Code as Creative Medium (Levin and Brain): body-named assignments (Personal Prosthetic in c10; the mini project is a Virtual Creature / Extrapolated Body in 3D) and variations at two depths for two tracks.
Processing Handbook: static before continuous (Part I builds in _ready; delta opens Part II in c16), a synthesis at the end of each part (c15, c28, c37).
The Nature of Code: the cumulative project is a museum exhibit of creatures; Ada's project_step puts each chapter's body into the student's hall of the endless museum.
Catlike Coding and the Book of Shaders: graph before surface (c13 visits WaveFunctions_Sine_Space early); construction as an axis; the shader as a single editable line (c22).
Gaboury, Image Objects: one technical object per chapter as a critical lens (the default body in c03, culling and the camera in c35, the GPU in c22).
SFPC Code Societies: a three-week critical format with a guest per session and small 'score' outcomes, the model for the short track's week 3.
UCSC AGPM 129 and Anthropy: make before the tool (the scan before any GDScript) and share a first work in week 1.

Gap named rather than borrowed [V via research_ccs]: none of these courses critiques geometry, bodies or VR; Ada's polycount-against-deformation, the blob, stretchability and impossible space are its own contribution.
